title: Shamrock Oil & Gas Corp. v. Sheets (1941)
summary: An original state-court plaintiff could not remove the action merely because the other party asserted a counterclaim against it.
notes:
This short assigned note does not provide a complete underlying transaction or litigation history. Its course function is identifying who may remove.

Shamrock, a non-Texas corporation, sued Sheets (doing business as Friona Independent Oil Co.), a Texas citizen, in Texas state court on a verified account; Sheets counterclaimed for more than $3,000 for breach of a separate contract, and Chief Justice Stone wrote for a unanimous Court that the removal statute's reference to 'defendants' means only the defendants to the original action, so a plaintiff cannot remove on the basis of a counterclaim.

Shamrock is the standard citation for strict construction of removal jurisdiction: due regard for the rightful independence of state governments requires federal courts to scrupulously confine their jurisdiction to the precise limits the statute defines.

sections.Parties: Shamrock Oil initiated the state-court action and later sought to remove after the defendant asserted a counterclaim.
sections.Material Facts: The party asking for a federal forum had voluntarily chosen the state court as plaintiff. Its removal theory relied on the fact that it was now defending a counterclaim. The precise classification of party roles under the statute, rather than ordinary language describing who defended a claim, controlled.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court rejected removal by the original plaintiff. The casebook presents the decision as a statutory limitation on the class of parties authorized to remove.
sections.Issue: Does a counterclaim make an original plaintiff a “defendant” entitled to remove the action?
sections.Holding: No. The statutory permission did not extend to the original plaintiff in that position.
sections.Reasoning: Removal authority is defined by Congress. Treating every party facing an adverse claim as a removable defendant would expand the statute beyond its established allocation and allow a plaintiff to withdraw its own choice of state forum when litigation became less favorable. Home Depot later applies related reasoning to a third-party counterclaim defendant.

learning.why: An original state-court plaintiff could not remove the action merely because the other party asserted a counterclaim against it.

topics.cp-removal: The original plaintiff could not remove by treating itself as a defendant to a counterclaim. The removal statute’s defendant designation depended on the party’s position in the original action.
topics.cp-usc-1441: The case construes the removal statute's word 'defendant' and is the source of the strict-construction rule for § 1441.
topics.cp-counterclaim: It establishes that a counterclaim does not make the original plaintiff a 'defendant' entitled to remove.
topics.cp-statute-interpretation: Shamrock is a standard example of strictly construing jurisdictional statutes against federal jurisdiction.

mnemonic.rationale: A counterclaim that could not remove
